papers.selection_reason: Learns interaction patterns from human-object demonstrations to guide reinforcement learning for bimanual dexterous manipulation.
papers.title: PatternDex: Learning Interaction Patterns to Guide Reinforcement Learning of Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation of Articulated Objects
papers.tldr: PatternDex learns object-driven interaction patterns from human demonstrations to guide embodiment-aware reinforcement learning for successful bimanual dexterous manipulation.

papers.abstract: Force-aware manipulation typically relies on specialized force or tactile sensors. We show that force-aware manipulation can instead be achieved through visual force prediction from the deformation of a compliant Fin Ray gripper. Our approach trains two models. First, we train a visual force estimator on calibration data and use it to annotate task demonstrations with force estimates. Second, we train an action--force proposal policy on these force-augmented demonstrations to jointly generate candidate robot actions and their associated forces. At test time, we sample candidate actions and the forces they are expected to produce, then execute the action whose predicted force is closest to a target from the demonstrations. We evaluate our approach on berry picking, empty-can grasping, in-hand reorientation, and plug insertion. Our results show that visual force prediction can guide inference-time action selection for contact-rich manipulation without requiring force or tactile sensors at deployment.
authors: Haonan Chen, Feiyang Wu, Yuxiang Ma, Mustafa Mete, Pengfei Ye, Junxuan Shen, Cheng Zhu, Aurora Ruggeri, Kelvin Cheung, Jiayuan Mao, Edward Adelson, Jiajun Wu, Robert D. Howe, Yilun Du
bullets: Replaces specialized force/tactile sensing with visual force prediction from a compliant gripper’s deformation.
Trains a visual force estimator to annotate demonstrations with estimated forces.
Learns an action–force proposal policy that generates candidate actions and predicted forces.
At test time, selects the action whose predicted force best matches a target force from demonstrations.
Evaluated on berry picking, empty-can grasping, in-hand reorientation, and plug insertion.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of visual force estimation and inference-time force search. (a) Visual force estimation converts a wrist-camera image into a masked Sobel edge representation and uses gφ to estimate the axial interaction force from the visible deformation of the compliant Fin Ray gripper. (b) During inference-time force search, the policy jointly samples candidate end-effector actions and force values. We execute the action from the sample whose generated force value most closely matches the target force.

Fig. 7. Representative successful rollouts of four force-sensitive manipulation tasks using force-based candidate selection. Each row shows a task sequence progressing from left to right. For empty soda can grasping and berry picking, the robot applies sufficient gripping force to lift and transfer the object without crushing it. During in-hand reorientation, the robot maintains contact while allowing the metal plate to pivot into an upright configuration. During plug insertion, the robot maintains sufficient contact friction to prevent slippage and fully inserts the plug into the socket.
Fig. 5. Manipulation success rates. Success rate (%) over 15 trials per task for single-sample policy inference and our force-search method, both using the same policy checkpoint.

Fig. 3. Hardware setups used in our experiments. (a) Visual force data collection setup, where an Intel RealSense D405 camera observes the deformation of the hand-held Fin Ray gripper and a six-axis F/T sensor records the ground-truth interaction force through 3D-printed contact fixtures. (b) The six-axis F/T sensor and 3D-printed contact fixtures used to record ground-truth interaction force during data collection. (c) Robotic manipulation platform used for policy evaluation, consisting of an ARX robotic arm equipped with wrist and side-view cameras.

Fig. 4. Force-estimation accuracy. (a) Reference load cell. (b) Force trajectories. (c) Estimated versus measured force (three episodes, 442 frames); dashed line: perfect agreement. Mean episode MAE: motor current, 4.20N; ViewForce, 0.91N (equal episode weights).

Fig. 1. Force-aware manipulation from visual gripper deformation. Humans naturally regulate force when handling fragile objects (left). We use wrist-camera observations of a compliant gripper (right, inset) to infer interaction force from visible deformation and enable gentle robotic manipulation without dedicated force or tactile sensing at deployment.

Fig. 8. Force Search. Distribution of 32 force predictions sampled from the policy for a held-out soda-can observation. The teal star marks the prediction selected by force search (4.45N). Points are offset vertically for readability.

Fig. 6. Representative failure modes under single-sample policy inference. From top left to bottom right: a dented empty soda can, a crushed berry, unsuccessful in-hand reorientation, and plug slippage within the gripper. These examples correspond to the four tasks reported in Fig. 5.

papers.selection_reason: Learns force-aware manipulation from visual gripper deformation and uses force-guided action selection for contact-rich robot tasks.
papers.title: Robot Learning with Visual Predicted Force
papers.tldr: A vision-based system predicts gripper forces from Fin Ray deformation and uses them to select actions for contact-rich robot manipulation without deployment-time force or tactile sensors.

papers.abstract: Memory is essential for long-horizon robotic manipulation, where successful actions may depend on past events that are no longer recoverable from the current observation. As episodes grow longer, however, retaining the full history becomes increasingly costly, creating a fundamental scalability challenge for memory-augmented policies. Existing approaches address this challenge by either storing selected past observations in a bounded memory bank or compressing interaction history into a fixed-size parametric state through Test-Time Training (TTT). Yet these formulations do not explicitly distinguish between historical information that can already be recovered from the policy's current context and information that must persist beyond it. We introduce TTT-RM, which repurposes TTT as Residual Memory, using fast weights not to generically compress history but to complement a bounded memory bank by preserving task-relevant historical information that cannot be recovered from the policy's current context. Concretely, TTT-RM learns a history decoder that reconstructs historical representations from the current observation and retrieved memory. The resulting reconstruction residual captures what this context fails to explain and serves as the learning target for TTT. The TTT slow weights are optimized against this residual target so that online fast-weight updates learn to encode complementary historical information over time. The fast-weight state is then queried to produce a residual memory representation that conditions action generation. Extensive experiments on memory-intensive simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks show that TTT-RM consistently improves across multiple memory designs, outperforms diverse baselines, and supports sustained execution on a three-minute, eight-stage stowing task.
authors: Haoxuan Wang, Gengyu Zhang, Ramana Rao Kompella, Gaowen Liu, Yan Yan
bullets: Addresses the scalability challenge of remembering task-relevant events during long-horizon manipulation.
Uses a bounded memory bank plus a history decoder to identify unrecoverable information as a reconstruction residual.
Trains Test-Time Training fast weights online to encode this residual and conditions action generation on the resulting representation.
Experiments across simulation and real-world tasks show consistent improvements across memory designs and baselines.
Demonstrates sustained execution on a three-minute, eight-stage stowing task.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Real-world results. Qualitative rollouts across the three manipulation tasks are paired with quantitative task progress profiles, which report the fraction of trials reaching or exceeding each progress threshold. Our method consistently achieves better performance across all task stages.

Figure 3: Ablation studies. (a) shows the effect of the residual-loss weight λres. Disabling residual supervision (λres = 0) can degrade performance, while moderate values yield the strongest results. (b) compares TTT-RM with a naive EM+TTT combination, showing that simply adding TTT to an EM-equipped policy provides limited benefit. (c) examines the effect of our three-stage training pipeline, with the full procedure achieving the best performance across both EM variants.

Figure 2: Overview of TTT-RM. Frozen visual features are selectively stored in Explicit Memory and written into TTT fast weights through the visual-stream writer. During training, the history decoder estimates what past information is recoverable from the existing policy context, and its reconstruction residual supervises Residual Memory. At inference, the decoder is removed, while Explicit Memory and Residual Memory jointly condition action generation.

Figure 1: Comparison of memory paradigms. Incoming observations are represented as tokens along the timeline. (a) Explicit Memory retains selected historical information in a bounded memory bank, giving direct access to only a sparse subset of the preceding history. (b) Test-Time Training instead compresses history into a fixed-size fast-weight state whose size does not grow with episode length. (c) TTT as Residual Memory. TTT is repurposed to preserve only the historical information not recoverable from the current observation and retrieved memory.
Table 1: Results on RoboMME. Performance is measured as average success rate (%). Each TTT-RM variant augments the corresponding Explicit Memory baseline with Residual Memory.
Table 2: Results on RMBench. Performance is measured as average success rate (%).

papers.selection_reason: Repurposes Test-Time Training as Residual Memory to preserve task-relevant historical information for long-horizon robotic manipulation tasks.
papers.title: Test-Time Training as Residual Memory for Robot Policies
papers.tldr: TTT-RM augments bounded robot-policy memory with test-time-trained fast weights that retain only historical information missing from the current context.

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow models provide expressive policy classes for online reinforcement learning (RL), enabling multimodal behaviors and improved performance. However, training these policies remains challenging: the critic specifies the desired policy as an unnormalized Boltzmann density but does not provide direct samples from it. Many existing methods rely on importance sampling to construct training signals, which can suffer from high variance, increasing computational cost and destabilizing training. We propose Score-Calibrated Flow (SCF), a simple and efficient algorithm for training generative models to sample from unnormalized densities without importance sampling or backpropagation through the sampling trajectory. We learn the desired flow by enforcing self-consistency, bypassing target posterior mean estimation. By jointly exploiting the prescribed target score and the structure of flow matching, we establish these self-consistency requirements as score-calibrated optimality conditions, first for the terminal density and then for the trainable velocity field. We prove that their unique solutions are, respectively, the target density and the ideal flow model that conditional flow matching (CFM) would recover if target samples were available. We formulate the velocity condition as a fixed-point equation and exploit its conditional-expectation structure to construct a stop-gradient objective for enforcing it. The resulting training procedure retains the scalable sample-interpolate-regress structure of CFM despite the absence of target samples, using endpoints generated by the current flow. For online RL, the critic gradient supplies the target score at the generated actions, yielding a direct approach to actor training. Experiments on RL benchmarks demonstrate that SCF matches or improves upon state-of-the-art generative-policy baselines, while substantially reducing training time.
authors: Zeyang Li, Yunan Wang, Risheek Garrepalli, Mohammad Ghavamzadeh, Navid Azizan
bullets: Addresses high-variance importance sampling when training diffusion or flow policies from unnormalized Boltzmann targets.
Uses target scores and flow-matching self-consistency to learn the desired terminal density and velocity field without target samples.
Implements a stop-gradient fixed-point objective with the scalable sample–interpolate–regress structure of conditional flow matching.
In online RL, critic gradients provide the target score for direct actor training.
Experiments on RL benchmarks report competitive or improved performance over generative-policy baselines with substantially lower training time.

papers.selection_reason: Generative flow-based policy learning for online RL is directly relevant to learned embodied/robot policy learning.
papers.title: Score-Calibrated Flow for Sampling from Unnormalized Densities with Applications to Generative Online Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Score-Calibrated Flow trains generative policies to sample from critic-defined, unnormalized RL densities without importance sampling or trajectory backpropagation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) often degrade under out-of-distribution task variations despite retaining partial task capability. To recover such capability, we propose RoboIRS, an inference-time internal representation steering method that uses successful and failed rollouts to train linear classifiers, select outcome-relevant intervention locations, and derive task-specific steering directions without updating policy parameters. On 15 simulation tasks with a frozen $\pi 0.5$ policy, RoboIRS improves the average success rate from 44.4% to 66.2%, outperforming alternative inference-time intervention baselines while adding little inference time. We further validate RoboIRS on real-robot manipulation using the same $\pi 0.5$ policy and demonstrate its applicability to a world-action model Cosmos Policy, where the average success rate improves from 35.4% to 55.4%. These results show that directly steering internal robot-policy representations can improve the performance of robot policies at inference time. Project website is available at https://rollingoat.github.io/roboirs/.
authors: Jiuzhou Lei, Chang Liu, Dayou Li, Zhiyuan Zhang, Xiao Liang, Yu She, Zhiwen Fan, Minghui Zheng
bullets: Targets degraded performance on out-of-distribution task variations while preserving existing policy capabilities.
Trains linear classifiers on successful and failed rollouts to identify outcome-relevant intervention locations and task-specific steering directions.
On 15 simulation tasks with a frozen π0.5 policy, raises average success from 44.4% to 66.2% with little added inference time.
Also improves real-robot manipulation and Cosmos Policy performance, raising Cosmos Policy’s average success from 35.4% to 55.4%.
Scope: evaluated on simulated and real-robot manipulation with π0.5 and on a world-action model; policy parameters remain frozen.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the proposed RoboIRS framework. (a) RoboIRS intervenes between transformer blocks by adding a scaled steering vector to the selected residual-stream representation without updating the policy parameters. (b) To construct the steering vector, residual-stream representations are collected from successful and failed rollouts and used to train a linear classifier. The classifier weight provides the steering direction that is injected into the residual stream during inference.
Fig. 1: Real-robot setup under visual distribution shift (top) and baseline comparison (bottom).
Fig. 4: t-SNE visualization of the last-layer’s residuals. Each panel compares residual representations from unsteered and steered policies separately for successful and failed rollouts.
Fig. 3: Steering strength vs. SR from a few tasks to show the typical patterns: monotonic increase/decrease; increase at moderate strengths before degrading at larger strengths.

TABLE I: Success rates (%) of unsteered and steered π0.5. Bold indicates improvements larger than one unsteered standard deviation for LIBERO-PRO. The Sign column denotes the steering direction s. Parentheses in the real-robot rows denote successes/total trials.
TABLE IV: Task-level success rates (%) of the unsteered and steered Cosmos Policy. Improvements exceeding one standard deviation of the unsteered policy are shown in bold.

TABLE III: Comparison of task-level success rates (%) and average inference time among baselines and RoboIRS. The highest task-level success rate is shown in bold. Win Margin reports the average success-rate difference over tasks where either the corresponding baseline or RoboIRS performs better; the number of winning tasks is shown in parentheses.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces RoboIRS, an inference-time method to steer internal representations of generalist robot policies using successful/failed rollouts without parameter updates.
papers.title: RoboIRS: Inference-Time Internal Representation Steering for Generalist Robot Policies
papers.tldr: RoboIRS improves out-of-distribution robot-policy performance at inference time by steering internal representations using successful and failed rollouts, without updating policy parameters.

papers.abstract: Actor-critic methods reuse past experience to improve sample efficiency. However, historical data are typically regarded as off-policy samples for the current policy-improvement update. This work introduces Regularized Dual Averaging Actor Critic (RDA2C), which assigns a distinct role to replay. In regularized dual averaging, the subsequent policy is determined by accumulated policy-improvement feedback, so historical advantage estimates contribute directly to the actor objective rather than solely to the most recent update. RDA2C stores state-action samples with critic-estimated advantage labels, fits a dual score model $Z_\theta$ to the aggregated dataset, and derives the current policy from the accumulated score model using the entropy mirror map. In this way, replay defines an empirical dual objective from which the policy is computed. To analyze RDA2C, we establish a finite-time value-gap decomposition, separating the regularized dual-averaging term from errors due to stale-replay supervised fitting, critic bias, finite-buffer variance, and replay coverage, and stating the assumptions under which each error is bounded. RDA2C accepts advantage labels from any critic. With GAE labels, RDA2C outperforms PPO on six of eight MuJoCo tasks and eight of twelve Atari games. RDA2C also outperforms AAPDA, the closest dual-averaging baseline, on six of eight MuJoCo tasks. With twin-$Q$ labels, RDA2C matches SAC at matched batch size and update frequency.
authors: Nianli Peng, Geoffrey J. Gordon, Kiant\'e Brantley
bullets: Reframes replay: historical advantage estimates directly shape future policy updates rather than serving only as off-policy samples.
Fits a dual score model to replayed state-action samples with critic-estimated advantage labels, then derives the policy through an entropy mirror map.
Provides a finite-time value-gap decomposition covering stale-replay fitting, critic bias, finite-buffer variance, and replay-coverage errors.
With GAE labels, RDA2C outperforms PPO on 6/8 MuJoCo and 8/12 Atari tasks, and outperforms AAPDA on 6/8 MuJoCo tasks.
With twin-Q labels, RDA2C matches SAC under matched batch size and update frequency.

figures.caption: Figure 2: RDA2C improves over matched PPO on six of eight MuJoCo tasks and over AAPDA on six of eight. Bars show per-environment relative improvement, 100 · (R̄ours − R̄base)/|R̄base|. Left: PPO matched to RDA2C’s architecture and hyperparameters (GAE labels, online return). Right: AAPDA at its released defaults (deterministic evaluation). Exact values: Appendix B.

Figure 3: RDA2C improves over PPO on eight of twelve Atari games. Bars show relative improvement over PPO, 100·(R̄RDA2C−R̄PPO)/|R̄PPO|, after 10M frames. The value axis is broken between +95% and +235%. The bars for BeamRider-v5, Enduro-v5, and Seaquest-v5 continue in the right segment. Exact mean ± std values are reported in Appendix B, Table 9.

Figure 11: Sensitivity to standard SAC replay buffer size. We vary the ordinary SAC replay buffer and keep the RDA label window fixed at 12,800. Returns are min-max normalized independently within each environment across all method and buffer configurations before aggregation. Error bars denote task SEM. InvertedPendulum is omitted from the normalized aggregate because it is saturated for every setting.

Figure 13: RDA2C gradient boosting learning curves. On CartPole-v1 (left), both xgb_dagger and xgb_boosting reach 500 within 106 steps. On Acrobot-v1 (right), xgb_dagger is slightly more sample efficient early, and both methods converge similarly by 106 steps.

papers.abstract: A vision--language--action (VLA) policy can complete complex tasks while ignoring the evidence that should determine its actions. An object held near the wrist camera can displace the instructed target. Language and action show the same pattern: a familiar noun can trigger the operation it was paired with in training even after the verb changes, and a gripper that closed on nothing may lift anyway. We call these dependencies modality shortcuts: regularities in successful demonstrations make visual, lexical, or motor cues sufficient to predict expert actions without the task evidence needed for the underlying decision. More demonstrations of the same kind can raise task success while leaving these shortcuts intact. We propose Perturbot which makes task-relevant evidence easier to use and shortcuts insufficient on their own: it applies task-preserving wrist-view perturbations, enriches instructions with decision-relevant captions, and adds random and failed trajectory segments relabeled with the behavior they contain. It complements scaling by changing what is scaled, and leaves inference unchanged. Moreover, we propose GroundingFscore, an offline score that diagnoses how severely a policy relies on modality shortcuts. Task success rate shows whether a policy improves, while GroundingFscore reveals whether the policy scales healthily, relying on task evidence rather than shortcuts. Together, Perturbot and GroundingFscore provide a training-and-evaluation framework for disentangling VLA decisions from shortcut priors while preserving responsiveness to task-relevant evidence.
authors: Mingyu Liu, Chonghao Sima, Tianjian Feng, Hanqing Wang, Cong Chen, Hao Chen, Chunhua Shen
bullets: VLA policies may succeed by exploiting modality shortcuts instead of evidence needed for the underlying task decision.
PerturbBot uses task-preserving wrist-view perturbations, decision-relevant instruction captions, and relabeled random or failed trajectory segments.
The method changes training while leaving inference unchanged, complementing model scaling by improving the data and signals being scaled.
GroundingFscore provides an offline measure of shortcut reliance alongside task success, helping assess whether scaling is healthy.
The framework aims to preserve responsiveness to task-relevant evidence while disentangling decisions from shortcut priors.

papers.abstract: Soft robots present significant modelling challenges due to their non-linearity, complex dynamics and potentially intricate geometries. These difficulties in accurate system identification and dynamics modelling limit their applications in precise robotics tasks. Prior modelling approaches typically suffer from trade-offs in accuracy, computational efficiency, or speed. The differentiable finite element method (FEM) offers a promising balance between these desiderata for soft robot modelling, and enables the use of gradients for efficient calibration and trajectory optimisation. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end differentiable FEM-based framework designed to streamline modelling and system identification for pneumatic soft robots, enabling the generation of reliable models for downstream tasks. The framework automates the conversion of computer-aided designs into voxelised tetrahedral viscoelastic FEM meshes that accurately represent the robot's geometry and actuation mechanism. By integrating easily acquired point cloud data with differentiable FEM, the framework achieves precise identification of material and dynamic actuation parameters using a minimal experimental setup. Additionally, the differentiable nature of the model facilitates trajectory optimisation by leveraging gradients from robot dynamics and contact interactions. We validate the framework by modelling a complex bellow-shaped pneumatic soft robot and demonstrate its efficacy in real-world motion planning tasks. Experimental results indicate high modelling accuracy, with a maximum positional error of less than 3 mm, and successful application in tasks such as path following and grasping.
authors: Shaohong Zhong, Yao Yao, Perla Maiolino, Ingmar Posner
bullets: Addresses the accuracy–efficiency trade-off in modelling nonlinear pneumatic soft robots.
Automatically converts CAD designs into voxelised tetrahedral viscoelastic FEM meshes representing geometry and actuation.
Uses differentiable FEM and point-cloud measurements to identify material and dynamic actuation parameters with minimal experiments.
Supports gradient-based trajectory optimisation involving robot dynamics and contact interactions.
Validated on a complex bellow-shaped robot with positional error below 3 mm, achieving path following and grasping.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical control architectures are widely used to decompose complex control problems into interacting control levels and are particularly important in robotics, where planning, whole-body motion, and lower-level control must be coordinated across different levels of abstraction and time scales. Their overall closed-loop performance, however, depends strongly on parameters distributed across the hierarchy, such that tuning controllers on different levels independently may neglect relevant cross-layer interactions. We propose a contextual Bayesian optimization framework for joint parameter learning in hierarchical control systems. Rather than modeling closed-loop performance only as a scalar black-box function, we retain separate observations of task performance, realization quality, and control effort. A correlated multi-output Gaussian process models these performance components, while their known aggregation into the overall closed-loop objective is evaluated analytically. The formulation exploits three complementary consequences of hierarchical control: informative performance quantities exposed by the hierarchy, coupling between parameters of different controller levels, and variations of these relations with operating conditions. We evaluate the approach for humanoid loco-manipulation, jointly tuning a centroidal predictive controller and a whole-body controller for physical box pushing under varying box mass. The proposed method achieves the lowest mean empirical regret during both training and adaptation among the considered baselines.
authors: Sebastian Hirt, Lukas Theiner, Jan Peters, Rolf Findeisen
bullets: Independent tuning can miss interactions between parameters at different control levels in hierarchical robotics systems.
The method uses a correlated multi-output Gaussian process and analytically combines predicted performance components into the overall objective.
It exploits hierarchy-exposed metrics, cross-level parameter coupling, and operating-condition-dependent relationships.
Evaluated on humanoid box pushing, it jointly tunes centroidal predictive and whole-body controllers under varying box mass.
It achieves the lowest mean empirical regret during training and adaptation among the evaluated baselines.

papers.abstract: Robots need to anticipate how their actions will change the world, since manipulation success hinges on the resulting contacts and object motions. However, existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies that predict future observations from shared features leave the forecast decoupled from the actions the policy will actually execute, and impose no physical constraints on how the scene may evolve. We introduce ForeAct3D, a framework for policy-grounded future world modeling within VLA policies. Learnable geometric queries decode depth, semantic segmentation, and camera pose from the policy representation into current and future semantic 3D scene states, and the future queries are conditioned on the policy-generated action chunk to ground the forecast in the planned interaction. A physical-consistency closure relates the two states through background staticity and instance-level rigidity, and anchors the wrist-camera pose to end-effector kinematics. These objectives shape the shared representation used for action generation during training, and no future prediction is required at inference. Without robot pretraining, ForeAct3D achieves 98.3\% average success on LIBERO and an average task length of 3.73 on CALVIN, outperforming its base policy on every suite. Ablations show that semantic 3D supervision, physical consistency, and action conditioning each improve manipulation performance, and that action conditioning substantially improves future object localization. Real-world experiments on spatial placement, object insertion, and sequential manipulation further raise average success from 6.7\% to 37.8\% over the base policy. The project page and code are available at https://github.com/anthonytao80-crypto/ForeAct3D.
authors: Zhe Tao, Feiran Wang, Gaowen Liu, Ramana Rao Kompella$, Yan Yan
bullets: Addresses forecasts that are decoupled from executed actions and lack physical constraints.
Uses geometric queries to predict depth, semantics, and camera pose for current and future 3D scene states.
Conditions future prediction on action chunks and enforces background staticity, object rigidity, and wrist-camera kinematics.
Future modeling shapes training representations but is not required during inference.
Improves simulation and real-world manipulation performance over the base policy, with gains supported by ablations.

papers.abstract: Designing effective reward functions in RL typically requires substantial expertise and trial and error. Recent work automates this process with LLM-based systems that generate and iteratively improve reward code using policy feedback. However, these methods are often hard to compare because they differ in implementation details, feedback assumptions, and evaluation environments. To address this, we introduce a Benchmark for Iterative Reward Design (BIRD) that expresses existing methods in a unified configuration and evaluation space. This lets us compare algorithms directly, ablate individual design choices, and prototype new components under matched feedback conditions and policy-training budgets. Across MuJoCo, Meta-World, Assistax, and HumanoidBench, we identify a small set of simple design choices that consistently improve performance. Combining these choices yields significantly better performance than the evaluated methods from prior work. Our results highlight the strength of simple baselines and motivate further study of when additional algorithmic complexity improves iterative reward design. Code is available at https://github.com/safety-research/bird.
authors: Logan Mondal Bhamidipaty, Lauren Robson, Linda Petrini, Shengrui Lyu, Kamal Ndousse
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of fairly comparing iterative reward-design algorithms due to differing implementations, feedback assumptions, and evaluation settings.
Introduces a unified configuration and evaluation framework supporting direct comparisons, ablations, and component prototyping under matched feedback and policy-training budgets.
Evaluates methods across MuJoCo, Meta-World, Assistax, and HumanoidBench.
Finds that combining consistently effective design choices outperforms the evaluated prior methods and underscores the strength of simple baselines.
Motivates further investigation into when added algorithmic complexity benefits iterative reward design.

papers.selection_reason: Unified benchmark for LLM-driven iterative reward design evaluated on robot RL environments (MuJoCo, Meta-World, HumanoidBench), transferable to robot policy learning pipelines.
papers.title: A Bird's-Eye View of Iterative Reward Design
papers.tldr: BIRD unifies and benchmarks LLM-based iterative reward-design methods, revealing that a few simple design choices can substantially improve performance across diverse RL environments.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires inferring task-relevant states from past interactions when the current observation alone is insufficient to determine the appropriate action. Despite progress in benchmarking memory-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) models, application-oriented tasks requiring history-dependent semantic inference remain underrepresented. We introduce GiT (Grounded in Time), a dataset and benchmark for grounding manipulation decisions in past events across biolaboratory, household, and industrial scenarios. It includes real-robot and Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) style demonstrations covering 18 bimanual tasks, together with simulation data and a ManiSkill-based evaluation suite covering nine tasks. Fine-grained subtask annotations and annotated counterfactual task pairs, in which similar current observations require different actions depending on prior events, support policy learning and targeted evaluation of history use. Evaluations of representative end-to-end VLA models in simulation and on selected real-world tasks reveal substantial room for improvement in history-dependent manipulation. The dataset and benchmark are available at the project page.
authors: Yi Wang, Yang Yang, Guangqi Xu, Sumin Lin, Ning Kang, Pengxiang Lu, Xiaotong Chen, Zeyu Xue, Ping Deng, Xing Liu, Chenguang Yang, Zhenyu Lu
bullets: Targets history-dependent semantic inference in robotic manipulation across biolaboratory, household, and industrial scenarios.
Combines real-robot, UMI-style, and simulation demonstrations spanning 18 bimanual tasks, with a ManiSkill evaluation suite covering nine tasks.
Provides fine-grained subtask labels and counterfactual task pairs where identical current observations require different actions based on history.
Evaluations of representative end-to-end VLA models show substantial room for improvement in temporal grounding, in simulation and selected real-world tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Dataset and benchmark for temporal grounding and history-dependent decision-making in robotic manipulation, targeting memory-augmented VLA models.
papers.title: Grounded in Time: A Multi-Source Dataset and Benchmark for Temporal Grounding in Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: GiT is a multi-source dataset and benchmark for evaluating whether robotic manipulation models can use past events to make decisions when current observations are ambiguous.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots could transport payloads substantially heavier than themselves by pulling passive wheeled vehicles instead of carrying the load. This capability, however, creates a coupled locomotion problem: the robot must maintain persistent upper-body contact while adapting to unknown, configuration-dependent forces arising from the payload, vehicle, and terrain. We present a whole-body control framework for humanoid rickshaw pulling that tracks commanded vehicle motion while preserving balance and stable grasps under uncertain load dynamics. During training, a privileged teacher exploits vehicle states, interaction forces, and load properties. Its actions and latent are distilled into a history-conditioned student that implicitly infers coupled dynamics from proprioceptive responses, followed by reinforcement-learning fine-tuning. Comparisons with \emph{No History} and \emph{Only History} baselines show that the resulting policy achieves accurate vehicle tracking while reducing vehicle oscillation, torso tilt, and actuation cost. Behavioral analysis shows that Unitree G1 propels the rickshaw and generates gait-synchronized whole-body reactions that stabilize its lateral and roll motions. Moreover, pulling redistributes joint effort and yields a lower robot-normalized cost-of-transport proxy than unloaded walking over most tested load--speed conditions. On hardware, a single policy performs starting, sustained pulling, turning, and stopping with both rigid payloads and human passengers, handling a loaded rickshaw mass of up to 115~kg without load-specific retuning. These results demonstrate robust heavy-load transportation through coordinated and persistent humanoid--vehicle interaction.
authors: Yangzhi Yang, Xiansheng Lin, Zhaoming Xie, Xiaobin Xiong
bullets: Addresses coupled locomotion under uncertain forces from the rickshaw, payload, and terrain.

Whole-body, gait-synchronized reactions stabilize lateral and roll motions while redistributing joint effort.
On hardware, one policy supports starting, pulling, turning, and stopping with rigid loads and passengers, including a rickshaw mass up to 115 kg without retuning.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a whole-body control framework for humanoid robots pulling wheeled loads, combining RL, teacher-student distillation, and hardware validation.

papers.tldr: A whole-body control policy enables a humanoid robot to pull heavy wheeled loads while maintaining balance, stable contact, and accurate vehicle motion.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in robot learning have enabled generalist control policies capable of completing a wide range of tasks. However, their performance degrades when deployed in unseen environments, making it critical to detect failures and teach recovery behaviors. Existing runtime monitoring methods often require task- and policy-specific training or hyperparameter tuning, limiting cross-task deployment and introducing additional overhead during iterative policy updates. We present Reward-DAgger, a robot-gated interactive imitation learning framework that uses dense progress signals from a general-purpose reward model to determine when human intervention is needed. Our approach is agnostic to the underlying policy architecture, requires no access to policy internals, and can be applied across tasks without retuning the gating mechanism. Our results show that Reward-DAgger achieves a better failure-detection accuracy-latency tradeoff than existing runtime monitoring baselines. Across eight simulated and real-world tasks, Reward-DAgger consistently improves the downstream policy's autonomous success rate throughout interactive learning and achieves strong return on human effort, outperforming the baselines in most settings. Importantly, the same gating configuration is used across tasks without task-specific hyperparameter tuning, demonstrating transfer across tasks, environments, and policy architectures. Code and videos are available at https://liralab.usc.edu/reward-dagger.
authors: Ryan Li, Yigit Korkmaz, Erdem B{\i}y{\i}k
bullets: Addresses failures of generalist robot policies in unseen environments by detecting when recovery teaching is needed.
Uses dense progress signals from a general-purpose reward model as a robot-gated intervention mechanism.
Works across policy architectures without accessing policy internals or retuning the gating mechanism per task.
Across eight simulated and real-world tasks, improves autonomous success during interactive learning and offers a strong human-effort return.
Achieves a better failure-detection accuracy–latency tradeoff than runtime monitoring baselines, with transfer across tasks, environments, and policies.

papers.abstract: We introduce the first learned articulated body simulator based on a selective state space model (SSM), called PhysMamba. PhysMamba predicts next-frame full-body state from position, rotation, and joint-action history, without velocity inputs. We compare four architectures under partial- and full-observation inputs and three training protocols. The from-scratch rollout training protocol gives Mamba2 strong short- and mid-horizon accuracy under partial observation (s10 = 43 mm, 2/50 diverged), while the two-stage teacher-based rollout protocol stabilizes GRU but fails for Mamba2. With CUDA graph compilation, Mamba2 reaches 0.107 ms per frame (9,334 FPS) on an H100 GPU, within 1.1$\times$ of GRU's un-compiled throughput, adding under 1% latency to a 30 Hz HMR pipeline and enabling integration as a differentiable physics module for video-based mesh recovery.
authors: Haochuan Zhang, Sinisa Todorovic
bullets: Evaluates four architectures under partial and full observation across three training protocols.
From-scratch rollout training gives Mamba2 strong short- and mid-horizon accuracy under partial observation.
The teacher-based rollout protocol stabilizes GRU but fails for Mamba2.
CUDA-compiled Mamba2 runs at 0.107 ms per frame on an H100, adding under 1% latency to a 30 Hz HMR pipeline.
Supports integration as a differentiable physics module for video-based mesh recovery.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces PhysMamba, a learned articulated body simulator using state space models, which is a core topic in embodied AI and world models for dynamics prediction.
papers.title: PhysMamba: Selective State Space Models as Learned Articulated Body Simulators
papers.tldr: PhysMamba applies selective state space models to fast learned articulated-body simulation from position, rotation, and joint-action histories without velocity inputs.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) inherit strong semantic grounding from pretrained vision-language backbones but are typically optimized for predicting actions rather than future observations. They can see and act, but they do not imagine the future before acting. World action models (WAMs) built on video diffusion backbones can imagine but treat language as frozen conditioning on a continuous latent space. Unified models bring these modalities into one architecture, but they either decode autoregressively, one token at a time, or keep video continuous with an auxiliary action head. In this work, we present SUAVE, a Single vocabulary Unified Action-Video modEl in which a masked diffusion transformer generates video and actions conditioned on language, with all three modalities represented as discrete tokens in a shared sequence. Choosing which tokens to mask at inference turns the same network into a world model, a robot policy, or a video-action model. For action-free co-training, the action positions of unlabeled video are filled with mask tokens and excluded from the loss. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate two findings. First, a single SUAVE model predicts long-horizon video and acts as a policy, competitive with dedicated world models and specialized action policies on static and dynamic manipulation tasks. On a real robot, our model generates subgoal images and an action chunk spanning one second of motion in 1,030 ms on an RTX 5090 GPU, sustaining closed-loop control at 2.5 actions per second. Second, pretraining on robot video and co-training on human video substantially improves policy performance and zero-shot robustness to distribution shift. Together, these results show that masked diffusion is a practical and versatile foundation for unified video-action modeling.
authors: Rhythm Syed, Jean Mercat, Sedrick Keh, Kushal Arora, Paarth Shah, Aykut Onol, Mengchao Zhang, Tony Dear
bullets: Addresses the gap between VLAs that act without imagining and world models that imagine without unified action generation.
Uses a masked diffusion transformer with language, video, and actions represented as discrete tokens in one sequence.
Masking different token types lets the same model function as a world model, policy, or video-action model.
Simulation and real-world experiments show competitive long-horizon prediction and manipulation control, including closed-loop operation at 2.5 actions/s.
Robot-video pretraining plus human-video co-training improves policy performance and robustness to distribution shift.

papers.abstract: Robots can acquire bad habits from a few defective moments in otherwise useful teleoperation. In mixed-quality robot data, normal and problematic demonstrations share most task behavior and differ only at a local action continuation. Full retraining is costly, while fine-tuning on clean data alone offers limited recovery under a small update budget. We ask whether the local difference can instead be fixed with only 1% of the full-training sample-backward budget. Using only episode-level retained/problematic labels, REDIRECT localizes the branch, assigns a coherent retained continuation to the original observations around it, and anchors shared behavior, without frame-level annotations or additional interaction. Across three randomized ManiSkill tasks and three seeds, REDIRECT raises the mean success rate from 68.2% to 90.3%, recovering 88.8% of the clean-retraining gap versus 22.1% for matched-compute fine-tuning. On a PiPER arm, it recovers 86.7-92.9% of the clean-only gap across cup insertion and towel folding. Local robot habits can therefore be repaired by spending the update budget on the behavioral difference rather than relearning shared behavior.
authors: Yu Zhang, Jiazhuo Li, Yancong Wei, Kangkang Dong, Xiaojun Zhu, Houde Liu
bullets: Targets defective local action continuations within otherwise useful teleoperation demonstrations.
Uses episode-level retained/problematic labels to localize the problematic branch, assign a retained continuation, and preserve shared behavior.
Across three randomized ManiSkill tasks, mean success increased from 68.2% to 90.3%.
Recovered 88.8% of the clean-retraining gap, compared with 22.1% for matched-compute fine-tuning.
On a PiPER arm, recovered 86.7–92.9% of the clean-only gap for cup insertion and towel folding.

papers.abstract: Recent world action models (WAMs) reuse pretrained video VAEs whose encoder latents directly condition downstream action policies. Quantization must therefore preserve not only reconstruction fidelity but also the policy-facing latent contract expected by the frozen policy. Direct NVFP4 leaves W4A4 quantization error uncompensated, whereas joint quantization-aware training (QAT) can recover reconstruction by moving this representation. On Wan2.1, joint QAT nearly matches FP32 VBench-7 (0.7403 versus 0.7409), yet LIBERO success collapses from 95.5% to 10.5%. Controlled decoder-only experiments show that activation quantize-dequantize operations alter the reconstruction signal and decoder Jacobian, redirecting the gradient returned to the encoder and inducing persistent latent drift. Based on this mechanism, we introduce LatentQuant, a two-stage NVFP4 QAT framework that first aligns the quantized encoder with its high-precision counterpart, then freezes it while adapting the decoder. Across Wan2.1 and Wan2.2, LatentQuant preserves near-baseline control and high reconstruction quality, achieving 95.75% success on LIBERO and 68.8% on RoboTwin. On NVIDIA B300 GPUs, NVFP4 execution achieves 1.17x-1.26x end-to-end VAE speedups over BF16 cuDNN.
authors: Ziye Deng, Lufang Chen, Shuyu Feng, Zhenwei Duan, Zicong Ye, Yu Sun, Xiaofan Li, Ruyi Gan, Hao Wang, Hao Zhang
bullets: WAMs require quantized VAE latents to remain compatible with frozen action policies, not merely reconstruct videos well.
Joint QAT can restore reconstruction quality but alters the policy-facing latent representation, reducing LIBERO success from 95.5% to 10.5%.
Decoder quantization changes reconstruction gradients and decoder Jacobians, causing persistent encoder latent drift.
LatentQuant first aligns the quantized encoder with its high-precision version, then freezes it while adapting the decoder.
Across Wan2.1 and Wan2.2, it achieves 95.75% LIBERO success, 68.8% RoboTwin success, and 1.17x–1.26x VAE speedups over BF16 cuDNN on B300 GPUs.

papers.abstract: This paper addresses autonomous landing of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) rotorcrafts on a heaving ship deck using a recurrent policy trained via asymmetric actor-critic reinforcement learning: the critic sees 6 s of future deck height during training, while the actor sees only what the onboard sensors provide in flight, a 17-dimensional state made of the vehicle's position, velocity and attitude relative to the deck and outputs world-frame velocity and yaw-rate commands. Training is performed across 4096 parallel simulated environments, followed by fine-tuning in 16 environments with an onboard vision pipeline in the loop. A control-barrier-function (CBF) stopping margin on the deck-relative vertical state is incorporated at two stages: as a reward term during training, where it halves the median simulated contact speed relative to a policy trained without it, and as a runtime safety filter at deployment, evaluated at every control step to abort and retry the descent when the margin is violated. Because the autopilot's disarm logic cannot detect the vehicle resting on a moving deck, proximity-based thrust cutoff at touchdown is commanded directly in the landing pipeline. The proposed approach is validated using a parallel-manipulator-platform-based deck emulator that reproduces the heaving motion of the ship deck (scaled to 0.70 m peak-to-peak, 7.5 s mean period) and a quadcopter UAV with an onboard camera. Across 31 motion-capture and 20 vision-based trials, the UAV landed every time, with median times to contact of 6.5 and 7.3 s; 77% and 50% landed on the first attempt, with mean deck-relative speeds of 0.29 and 0.27 m/s, respectively, at the instant of thrust cutoff, which is the last speed under the policy's control. Supplementary video: https://youtu.be/S5hDkrSZJt4
authors: Ritwik Shankar, Chiranjeev Prachand, Abhishek, Soumya Ranjan Sahoo
bullets: Uses asymmetric actor-critic training: the critic accesses future deck motion, while the flight actor relies only on onboard sensor observations.
Adds a control-barrier stopping margin during training and deployment; training reduced median simulated contact speed by half versus omitting the barrier term.
The deployment pipeline includes abort-and-retry safety filtering and proximity-based thrust cutoff because the autopilot cannot recognize touchdown on a moving deck.
Validated on a heaving deck emulator with motion-capture and vision-based sensing: all 51 trials achieved landing.
First-attempt success was 77% with motion capture and 50% with vision; mean deck-relative speeds at thrust cutoff were 0.29 and 0.27 m/s, respectively.

papers.abstract: Foundation models and large-scale human data provide rich sources of manipulation intent, but translating this intent into multi-fingered robot behavior remains difficult. Dexterous hands still lack a reusable low-level primitive that reliably establishes contact across tasks and embodiments. We propose GOTT, a reach-acquire-move framework built around a single cross-embodiment contact-acquisition primitive. Given a robot-agnostic object trajectory and a reach specification, GOTT first brings the hand near a task-relevant contact region. The shared closed-loop primitive then establishes stable contact from this approximate initialization, and a pose-conditioned controller tracks the desired object motion. Reach specifications may come from future-aware planning, external models, or human demonstrations, while the primitive and tracking backend remain unchanged. Simulation and real-world experiments show that GOTT is able to establish robust contact across diverse objects, arm-hand platforms, and seen and unseen hand morphologies. It also consistently improves end-to-end task success over open-loop grasp execution.

papers.abstract: In partially observable Markov decision processes, the optimal policy generally depends on the history of observations and past actions. Asymmetric actor-critic methods have become popular to learn such policies when additional information, such as the true state of the environment, is available during training. The critic, which is not needed at execution, is given access to the state. A critic conditioned on the state alone is generally ill-defined and yields biased policy gradients. Conditioning on the state and the history, the history-state critic restores both. In this paper, we show that conditioning the critic on the state and the policy's own memory, i.e., the internal representation of the history through which the policy selects its actions, is already well-defined and gives unbiased policy gradients, removing the need for a second recurrent approximator of the history. We call it the memory state critic. It follows that a critic based on the policy's memory need not backpropagate its loss into that memory, even though the memory is a lossy encoding of the history. We evaluate the memory-state critic in a vision-based pursuit-evasion environment between two quadrotors across two arena types. The pursuer is the learning agent, and the evader is sampled per episode from a fixed pool of heuristic behaviours. The results show that the memory-state critic outperforms the history-state critic and converges faster. In addition to being unbiased compared to the state-only critic, it maintains a slight edge in the wall arena, where the actor's history carries information that the privileged state alone does not.
authors: Arthur Louette, Alejandro S\'anchez Roncero, Gaspard Lambrechts, Pascal Leroy, Julien Hansen, Petter \"Ogren, Damien Ernst

Conditions the critic on environment state plus the actor’s memory representation of observation-action history.
Shows the critic’s loss need not backpropagate into the actor’s memory, despite that memory being lossy.
In vision-based quadrotor pursuit-evasion, it converges faster and outperforms the history-state critic across two arena types.
It retains a slight advantage in the wall arena, where actor history contains information unavailable from privileged state alone.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) leverage pretrained video foundation models for robot manipulation, but their large backbones and video-action co-prediction are expensive. Although existing acceleration techniques offer many ways to reduce this cost, selecting and composing them requires substantial engineering for each model and hardware platform. To tackle this bottleneck, we present WAMJET, an agentic harness that accelerates WAM inference by equipping coding agents with reusable optimization guidance and measurement and validation tools. WAMJET follows a bottleneck-driven workflow where the agent profiles inference, modifies targeted code, validates effects, and iteratively refines the acceleration stack as bottlenecks shift, while preserving action quality. Experiments span six WAMs, three coding agents, and two GPU architectures. WAMJET achieves up to 9.95x lossless speedup over upstream implementations. Approximation and hardware-aware optimization yield additional latency reductions, with comparable success rates. The results show that WAMJET can produce effective acceleration stacks for WAM deployment.
authors: Le Chen, Lixin Liu, Jan Schneider, Zeju Qiu, Simon Guist, Bernhard Sch\"olkopf, Dieter B\"uchler
bullets: Addresses the engineering burden of selecting and composing WAM acceleration techniques.
Uses coding agents with reusable optimization guidance, profiling, measurement, and validation tools.
Follows a bottleneck-driven loop: profile, target code changes, validate action quality, and refine as bottlenecks shift.
Evaluated across six WAMs, three coding agents, and two GPU architectures.
Reports up to 9.95× lossless speedup; approximation and hardware-aware optimizations provide further latency reductions with comparable success rates.

papers.abstract: Soft tactile sensors elevate robotic touch through enhanced flexibility and adaptability, yet most existing designs depend on embedded electronics that are susceptible to interference and environmental limitations. In this work, we leverage fluid-solid interactions to develop a class of soft tactile sensors that operate entirely without electronics at the sensing site. The sensor comprises a fluid-filled elastomeric channel connected to only two external pressure sensors. Touching different regions of the elastomeric surface displaces the viscous fluid, producing distinct pressure patterns that encode both touch position and force. These signals are decoded through a machine learning framework that integrates feature extraction, soft clustering, and adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference to achieve accurate localization and force estimation. We validate this concept through single-point touch localization and force estimation in a linear (1D) sensor and extend the same sensing principle to 2D tactile mapping by routing the channel across the surface using space-filling curves, while maintaining the same minimal hardware setup. This simple approach remains effective in environments where conventional electronic sensors often fail, such as underwater or in the presence of magnetic interference.
authors: Arman Goshtasbi, Minke Berghuis, Aida Parvaresh, Saravana Prashanth Murali Babu, Robert W. Style, Ahmad Rafsanjani
bullets: Addresses the environmental and interference limitations of electronics embedded in soft tactile sensors.
Uses a fluid-filled elastomeric channel with only two external pressure sensors; touch-induced fluid displacement creates informative pressure patterns.
Decodes signals with feature extraction, soft clustering, and adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference.
Demonstrates single-point localization and force estimation in 1D, and extends the same principle to 2D mapping via space-filling channel paths.
Maintains minimal hardware while supporting operation in settings such as underwater environments and magnetic interference.

papers.abstract: Discrete motion tokenizers encode motion as atomic units and are widely used for co-speech gesture generation. It remains unclear which motion properties, especially those relevant to gesture semantics, are recoverable from these codebooks. We probe a reconstruction-trained codebook using 19 co-speech gesture descriptors spanning from raw motion to abstract communicative function. Results show that geometry and handedness are readily decodable from token embeddings, while motion category is only weakly decoded despite showing systematic differences in discrete code usage. This gap between reconstruction quality and descriptor decodability suggests that reconstruction objectives alone do not guarantee that gesture semantics are captured, and that evaluating codebooks on such properties can guide the design of more semantic motion tokenizers.
authors: Varsha Suresh, Divij Jain, Jia Liu, M. Hamza Mughal, Vera Demberg
bullets: Geometry and handedness are readily decodable from token embeddings.
Motion category is only weakly decodable, despite systematic differences in code usage.
High reconstruction quality does not guarantee that codebooks encode gesture semantics.
Evaluating tokenizers on semantic descriptors may guide more meaningful codebook design.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms frequently compare probability distributions, such as state visitation distributions induced by policies and experts, action distributions from learned policies and offline datasets, or transition distributions from learned models and environments. However, commonly used divergences may become ineffective when these distributions overlap weakly, which is frequently encountered in imitation learning, offline RL, and deployment under distribution shift. Optimal transport (OT) offers an alternative by measuring the cost of \emph{moving} probability mass from one distribution to another under a ground cost that encodes task geometry. This survey covers how OT is used inside RL objectives and algorithms. For each method, we identify: the role OT plays, the distributions compared, the OT formulation used, and the treatment of temporal structure. Beyond categorising existing methods, we discuss the motivations behind different OT choices, practical considerations such as cost design and computational challenges, and highlight open problems including scalable trajectory-level transport, principled handling of mass mismatch, and theoretical analysis for OT-regularised RL.
authors: Yujie Zhu
Charles A. Hepburn
Matthew Thorpe
Giovanni Montana
bullets: Covers OT applications in imitation learning, offline RL, and deployment under distribution shift.
Categorizes methods by OT’s role, the distributions compared, the transport formulation, and treatment of temporal structure.
Explains why different OT formulations and ground-cost designs are chosen, alongside practical computational considerations.
Highlights open challenges in scalable trajectory-level transport, handling mismatched probability mass, and developing theory for OT-regularized RL.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Where optimal transport enters the RL pipeline. Each spoke represents a distinct role that OT plays, with the representative objective and section reference. Here W denotes a generic OT-based discrepancy, which may differ across applications, e.g., W1,W2 or an entropy-regularised formulation. Additional roles not shown include safety constraints (Sections 7.2, 7.3), preference alignment (Section 7.4), transfer and curricula (Sections 7.6, 8.3), and multi-policy/multi-agent diversity (Section 8).

Figure 2: The ground cost determines what OT counts as a good match. In both panels, the source and target marginals are the same, but the ground cost changes. Because OT minimises transport cost under that matrix, the optimal plan changes as well. This is why the ground cost is a modelling choice, not a numerical detail.

Figure 4: Example of optimal transport between two continuous distributions. The heatmap in the left figure shows the standard OT plan, and the right figure shows the entropy-regularised OT plan (ε = 0.01), which is smoother. Brighter colour indicates more mass is transported.

Figure 5: Three OT formulations. (a) Balanced OT enforces exact marginal constraints: all source mass reaches the target. (b) Partial OT transports only a fraction m of the total mass, leaving the rest unmatched (×)—useful when data contain outliers or suboptimal demonstrations (Section 6). (c) Unbalanced OT allows mass creation and destruction at a cost (red arrows), softly penalising marginal deviations rather than enforcing them exactly. Dot sizes indicate relative mass.

Figure 3: Offline reward labelling via optimal transport. An optimal coupling Γ∗ is computed between empirical state marginals of learner and expert trajectories, treating each as a uniform distribution over its states. This figure shows an example of a coupling, where each row sums to 1/T = 0.20; each column sums to 1/TE = 0.25. The reward at each learner state st is the negative transport cost to matched expert states under the optimal plan, r(st) = − ∑TE t′=1 c(st, s E t′ ) Γ∗ t,t′ . A near-diagonal structure emerges when trajectories are temporally aligned. The coupling in the figure is an example and is not necessarily the optimal coupling.

Figure 7: Standard vs. temporally-aware OT matching between learner and expert trajectories. (a) Without temporal constraints, the coupling can align temporally distant states, producing crossing matches that yield noisy pseudorewards. (b) With a band constraint |t − t′| ≤ 3 (or context-window costs), matches are near-diagonal, reducing spurious alignments while tolerating modest speed variation.

Figure 12: The Wasserstein ambiguity set for distributionally robust RL. The nominal transition P0(· | s, a) (dark-blue dot) sits at the centre of a Wasserstein ball Uδ = {P : Wp(P, P0) ≤ δ} inside the space of transition distributions P(S). Grey dots denote other candidate distributions inside the ball. The worst-case is represented by P ∗ (red dot). Two modelling choices shape this game: the ground metric d determines which perturbations are considered admissible (through the Wp geometry), while the radius δ controls how far models may move away from the nominal one, determining the conservatism of the resulting policy.

Figure 9: OT in model-based RL (Section 5). A learned world model Pϕ(· | s, a) is trained to match the true transitions under a Wasserstein loss that upper-bounds worst-case value error. Bisimulation metrics embed this comparison into a fixed-point state metric (Section 5.3).

Figure 6: OT in imitation learning and reward inference (Section 3). OT compares learner and expert behaviour distributions via dual critics or primal couplings, yielding shaping rewards or pseudo-reward labels (Sections 3.3–3.4). Temporal/intent-aware extensions modify the coupling or ground cost (Section 3.5); cross-domain settings use GW (Section 3.6).

Figure 11: OT in robustness, safety, and transfer (Section 7). A Wasserstein ambiguity set Uε around the nominal transitions defines worst-case Bellman updates (Section 7.1). OT-based visitation regularisation and preference alignment shape where the policy visits or how it aligns with human feedback (Sections 7.2–7.4).

Figure 8: OT in policy optimisation and regularisation (Section 4). Wasserstein trust regions constrain per-state action distributions or trajectory embeddings to stay close to a reference policy (Sections 4.2–4.4). Wasserstein-trained critics use OT losses on return or Q-value distributions (Section 4.5). The blue dashed bidirectional arrow connects two distributions compared by OT, while grey solid arrows represent connections in the RL algorithm.

OT enters as a behaviour constraint W(πθ(· | s), πβ(· | s)) that keeps the learned policy geometrically close to the data-generating policy with both induced distributions approximated by collected trajectories (Section 6.2). papers.abstract: Humanoid motion trackers can reproduce diverse whole-body motions, but their performance degrades on complex terrain where terrain-agnostic references become physically infeasible. We present PGMT, a Perceptive General Motion Tracking pipeline for humanoid robots that learns terrain adaptation from independently selected motion references and terrains. PGMT first learns a general tracking and recovery prior, then incorporates terrain perception through motion-conditioned terrain glimpses that selectively encode regions relevant to the current motion. Terrain-aware tracking relaxation allows necessary deviations from the reference while preserving its motion intent. Zero-shot deployment on a Unitree G1 demonstrates robust terrain-adaptive locomotion and whole-body motion execution over real-world terrain with obstacles up to 37 cm high, while supporting teleoperation, dynamic motion tracking, and fall recovery. PGMT extends general humanoid motion tracking beyond flat ground, providing a unified policy for terrain-adaptive locomotion, diverse whole-body behaviors, and teleoperation in complex environments. Project homepage: https://luyili.github.io/pgmt/
authors: Hongyi Li
Li Peizhuo

papers.abstract: This paper presents a soft robotic drummer for accurate and efficient drum rolls. High-frequency drum rolls require the "multi-bounce technique," where a drumstick bounces multiple times with a single stroke. In robotic reproduction of this technique, the body's elasticity is key, while the fine motion during the stroke is also crucial for maximizing the potential of that elasticity. Therefore, we design two tricks: i) Tap-Pull (TP) trick to increase the number of rebounds by adding a pulling motion after impact; and ii) Micro-Pulse (MP) trick to keep the drumming volume by injecting small oscillations during the stroke. Due to the nonlinear complexity of soft embodiment, both tricks are efficiently tuned using Bayesian optimization in a data-driven manner for accomplishing the respective objectives quantified. We evaluated the optimized behaviors with soft and rigid end-effectors. As a result, the soft TP achieved the highest bounce count (12.25 per stroke) with uniform intervals. The soft MP suppressed the volume decay, yielding 6.8-times higher acoustic efficiency compared to the rigid MP. These results indicate that the proposed tricks with the combination of elasticity and optimization can make robots play excellent drum rolls.

Takanori Jin
Taisuke Kobayashi

The soft Tap-Pull achieved 12.25 bounces per stroke, while soft Micro-Pulse delivered 6.8× higher acoustic efficiency than its rigid counterpart.

papers.abstract: Timed Partial Orders (TPOs), originally proposed for workflows, provide an interpretable framework for robot task specification with planning algorithms based on mixed-integer linear programming (MILP). However, TPOs are limited in expressivity, capturing only partial-order events with simple timing constraints. In this paper, we introduce Conditional TPOs (cTPOs), which extend TPOs with richer relative-timing constraints and conditional event activations based on environmental conditions. We show that planning for cTPOs also reduces to an MILP problem; however, the added expressivity results in significantly larger MILPs that can become computationally intractable. To address this challenge, we propose a decomposition algorithm that partitions a cTPO into smaller sub-TPOs, yielding a sequence of smaller MILP problems. We prove that this decomposition is complete and preserves plan optimality while improving the interpretability of complex tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of cTPOs as a task specification framework and the efficiency of our decomposition approach, achieving up to four orders of magnitude speedup over the monolithic MILP.

Morteza Lahijanian

Experiments show up to four orders of magnitude speedup over monolithic MILP planning.

papers.abstract: Deep learning is an efficient technique to monitor the real time welding process, reducing post-welding repairs and production delays. This paper leverages the monitoring capability by proposing a multi modal temporal attention based deep learning defect detection model for internal defects that are challenging to detect, including porosity, lack of penetration and fusion, undercut, and cold lap during Gas Metal Arc Welding in fillet joints. The model is trained on collected welding images and sound data from an industrial collaborative welding robot. The results show that the attention module can improve the F1 Score to 0.99. We use explainable Artificial Intelligence to interpret the proposed models behavior and dataset distribution, determining potential important areas in image and sound spectrograms and preferred modality to detect each defect. This improves trust and reliability in Artificial Intelligence driven welding inspection.

Mahyar Asadi
Klaske Van Heusden
Guy A. Dumont

Supports more trustworthy automated welding inspection and may reduce post-welding repairs and production delays.

papers.abstract: Inspired by human vision, we introduce a framework using active gaze to enable fine-grained bimanual manipulation with only a single stereo camera. EyeRobot 2.0 physically attends to a 3D fixation point in the scene by swiveling two eye viewpoints to center their gaze on it. The resulting images are processed foveally by allocating more visual tokens to the image centers, focusing computation on task-relevant features. Such Active Visual Fixation (AVF) requires carefully coordinated gaze during task execution, which we accomplish hierarchically by first training a low-level gaze servoing policy conditioned on a goal object, then training a target selector which emits fixation goals based on task progress. Both modules are trained with RL on real-world data: the first is trained with a dense geometric reward and the second co-trains with the BC gripper policy which allows it to discover fixation sequences that can resemble a human's fixation sequence while performing the task. EyeRobot 2.0 further takes advantage of fixation by canonicalizing gripper information into a fixation-relative SE(3) frame, which compacts the size of the action distribution to learn. We collect teleoperation data for 7 real-world and 6 simulated tasks, and conduct over 1000 physical and 1800 simulated robot trials comparing EyeRobot 2.0 against passive stereo and ego + wrist camera policies trained on the same data. Removing wrist cameras is costly for standard policies: with only passive stereo, real-world success drops from 52% to 27%. EyeRobot 2.0 closes this gap with only stereo, outperforming passive stereo by 40% in real and 20% in sim. It matches ego + wrist policies when their wrist views are clear (69% vs. 64%), and more than doubles their success when grasped objects occlude the wrist cameras (48% vs. 22%)
authors: Kush Hari, Justin Kerr, Nidhya Shivakumar, Samarth Mahapatra, Carmelo Sferrazza, Jiahui Lei, Jitendra Malik, C. Karen Liu, Ken Goldberg, Angjoo Kanazawa
bullets: Addresses the loss of visual information caused by removing wrist-mounted cameras during manipulation.
Swivels two eye viewpoints toward task-relevant 3D fixation points and allocates more visual tokens near image centers.
Hierarchically learns gaze servoing and fixation-target selection with reinforcement learning, alongside a behavioral-cloning gripper policy.
Canonicalizes gripper state relative to fixation, simplifying the action representation.
Across real and simulated tasks, it substantially outperforms passive stereo and matches or exceeds wrist-camera policies, especially when wrist views are occluded.

This target selector is trained with RL to maximize the prediction accuracy of a gripper BC policy, which is co-trained from scratch at the same time on viewpoints generated from the fixation rollout. Action chunks are supervised with teleop demos, and negative prediction error is supplied as the reward for the selector to optimize. (Right) Action chunks are represented as SE(3) chunks in the eye frame, aligned with the current fixation point.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in frontier models enable robot manipulation from only a few demonstrations, but high inference latency limits their use for real-time robot control. To bridge this gap, we study two complementary approaches that connect frontier reasoning with low-latency local execution. First, we use a frontier model to autonomously generate demonstrations that supplement human demonstrations for training a fast local policy. We augment its in-context examples with corrective demonstration segments that show how to recover from physical errors, improving generation reliability. Generation time and cost decrease as successful examples accumulate in context, suggesting a path toward more efficient data collection. At deployment, a harness combines frontier-generated instructions with a fast local policy, enabling efficient execution while preserving the frontier model's ability to guide and correct actions. With low-latency execution delegated to the local policy, the bottleneck shifts to its capacity to reliably follow the frontier model's diverse instructions. Our second bridge introduces dense language supervision across three nested granularities---primitive, atomic, and composite---with multi-aspect descriptions at each level. Across long-horizon tasks in RoboCasa 365 and BEHAVIOR-1K, where instructions change as execution progresses, the combined supervision achieves the highest performance under both oracle and frontier-model instructors, demonstrating more reliable instruction following through the policy's language interface. Finally, we evaluate both bridges together on a crossword task that combines semantic planning and manipulation within a fixed time budget. These results support autonomous demonstration generation and dense language supervision as complementary components for connecting frontier reasoning to low-latency local execution.

papers.abstract: Learning general-purpose robot policies requires large-scale real-world interaction data, yet collecting robot demonstrations remains expensive and difficult to scale. Egocentric videos offer abundant human interaction experience with task-relevant semantics for robotic manipulation, but direct transfer is challenging for two reasons: latent actions inferred from frame reconstruction can be dominated by nuisance variation such as ego-camera motion, and human and robot behaviors often exhibit different temporal dynamics. We propose WING (World Action Learning via INteraction-Centric Spectral Latent Guidance), a framework for transferring interaction knowledge from egocentric videos to robot policies. WING first separates observer-induced motion from hand-object interaction and distills the interaction-centric component into latent actions. It then exploits the observation that cross-embodiment task semantics are concentrated in slowly varying temporal structures, identifying shared low-frequency components between egocentric latent actions and robot behaviors in the spectral domain and using them to guide action generation. WING achieves average success rates of 99.20% on LIBERO, 93.80% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 57.7% on RoboCasa-GR1, and also performs strongly across four real-world manipulation tasks under diverse generalization settings. These results show that interaction-centric spectral guidance provides an effective and scalable way to transfer physical interaction knowledge from human egocentric video to robot control. Project page: https://mikuz12.github.io/wing/
authors: Zhiming Liu, Yikun Miao, Ying Chen, Hongrui Yin, Fangqi Zhu, Xiaoyi Pang, Quanxin Shou, Zhengyang Yan, Haodong Wang, Song Guo
